problems.stem: A traceability row reads: Principle = Mayer's signaling principle; Feature = "we added color." Which rewrite makes the row defensible?
options: Principle = signaling; Feature = we used a nicer color palette across the deck.
Principle = signaling; Feature = a yellow highlight cues the one term the narration is explaining at that moment, so attention is directed instead of left to scan the whole frame.
Principle = signaling; Feature = the slide looks more modern now.
Principle = signaling; Feature = AI suggested the color, so we kept it.
problems.explanation: Traceability requires the feature to be the operational mechanism of the principle. Signaling directs attention to essential material at the right moment, not decoration.

problems.stem: Which direction should a sound traceability argument run?
options: Feature to principle: build the feature you like, then find a principle that sounds like it justifies it.
Principle to feature: name the learning principle and the demand it addresses, then show the specific feature that operationalizes it.
Either direction works as long as both are named somewhere in the matrix.
Principle to aesthetic: pick the principle that matches the chosen visual style.
problems.explanation: Post-hoc principle-fitting rationalizes a feature you already wanted. Traceability is meaningful only when the principle and its demand drive the feature.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to map your storyboard features to multimedia principles. It returns a clean table citing the coherence and modality principles. What is the strongest bounded use?
options: Accept the table because every row cites a real principle.
Check each row for a controlling principle per feature and reject any row where the cited principle does not actually describe what the feature does to the learner's processing.
Add every principle the AI lists so the table looks thorough.
Ask the AI to also score each mapping out of ten and report the average.
problems.explanation: AI often attaches plausible-sounding principle labels that do not match the feature's actual mechanism. The designer must audit each mapping against the principle's real definition.

problems.stem: A reviewer notes that your matrix "maps every feature to three principles each." Why might this be a weakness rather than a strength?
options: Three principles per feature is always too many to defend.
Stacking many principles onto one feature often hides that the feature was not designed from any single principle's demand, making the mapping decorative rather than diagnostic.
Reviewers prefer one principle per matrix, not per feature.
It makes the matrix too long to fit on one page.
problems.explanation: Dense many-to-one mappings usually signal post-hoc labeling. A diagnostic matrix names the controlling principle and the demand it addresses, even if a feature touches others secondarily.
